objectives: Apply Nernst + Hodgkin-Huxley to cardiac action potential.

slides.title: Cardiac action potential + Nernst
slides.body:
Heart cells have specialized action potentials with distinct phases (ventricular myocyte, ~300 ms):
• **Phase 0** (depolarization): rapid Na⁺ inflow → membrane potential rises from -90 to +30 mV. Driven by voltage-gated Na channels.
• **Phase 1** (early repolarization): brief K⁺ efflux + Cl⁻ shifts.
• **Phase 2** (plateau, ~200 ms): Ca²⁺ inflow balances K⁺ outflow → sustained depolarization. This long plateau is unique to cardiac cells + allows full ventricular contraction.
• **Phase 3** (repolarization): K⁺ outflow dominates as Ca²⁺ channels close.
• **Phase 4** (resting): membrane back to -90 mV; ATP-driven Na/K pump restores ion gradients.

**Nernst equation** for an ion X:
  E_X = (RT/zF) × ln([X]_out/[X]_in)

At 37 °C: E_K ≈ -94 mV; E_Na ≈ +65 mV; E_Ca ≈ +130 mV.

**Resting potential** of -85 to -90 mV is dominated by K⁺ permeability + close to E_K.

**Action-potential propagation**: gap junctions connect adjacent myocytes electrically → conduction velocity ~1 m/s in ventricle. Specialized **conduction system**:
- Sinoatrial (SA) node: pacemaker; ~60-100 bpm intrinsic.
- Atrioventricular (AV) node: 0.1-s delay between atria + ventricles.
- Bundle of His + Purkinje fibers: fast conduction throughout ventricles for synchronized contraction (conduction velocity ~4 m/s).

Dysfunction at each level produces characteristic arrhythmias.

slides.title: 12-lead ECG: leads + waveform
slides.body:
**ECG** records electrical activity of the heart from the body surface. The 12-lead system:
• **Limb leads** (Einthoven 1903): I, II, III + augmented aVR, aVL, aVF.
• **Precordial leads**: V1-V6 across the chest.

Each lead has a view of the heart from a different angle → can localize abnormalities.

**Standard PQRST waveform** (1 cardiac cycle):
• **P-wave**: atrial depolarization (~80 ms, 0.1-0.3 mV amplitude).
• **PR interval**: P-wave start to QRS start (~120-200 ms). Measures AV-node delay.
• **QRS complex**: ventricular depolarization (~80-120 ms, 1-2 mV).
• **ST segment**: plateau between QRS + T (~80 ms, should be isoelectric).
• **T-wave**: ventricular repolarization (~150-200 ms, 0.2-0.5 mV; opposite polarity to QRS in many leads).
• **QT interval**: QRS start to T end (~350-450 ms, varies with HR; QTc corrected formulae).

**Normal ECG features**:
- Sinus rhythm: regular, P before every QRS, normal PR + QRS + QT.
- Heart rate 60-100 bpm.
- ST isoelectric.
- T-wave concordant with QRS (positive in lead II usually).

slides.title: Arrhythmias + clinical interpretation
slides.body:
**Conduction abnormalities**:
• **1st-degree AV block**: PR > 200 ms; every P followed by QRS. Often benign.
• **2nd-degree AV block** Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation → dropped QRS. Usually node-level.
• **2nd-degree AV block** Mobitz II: fixed PR; intermittent dropped QRS. Below-node lesion; can progress to complete block.
• **3rd-degree (complete) AV block**: P + QRS completely dissociated. Pacemaker required.
• **Bundle branch block (BBB)**: QRS > 120 ms; right (RBBB) vs left (LBBB) by morphology in V1-V6.

**Tachyarrhythmias**:
• **Sinus tachycardia**: rate >100; normal P + QRS. Physiological (exercise, fever) or pathological.
• **Atrial fibrillation (AFib)**: irregularly irregular; no discernible P-waves. ~30 million globally; major stroke risk.
• **Atrial flutter**: sawtooth P-waves; usually 2:1 or 4:1 AV conduction.
• **SVT (supraventricular tachycardia)**: narrow QRS, rapid rate.
• **Ventricular tachycardia (VT)**: wide QRS, rate 100+. Hemodynamic instability; can degenerate into VF.
• **Ventricular fibrillation (VF)**: chaotic + lethal; immediate defibrillation required.

**Ischemic ECG signs**:
- **ST elevation**: STEMI (transmural infarct); ≥1 mm in 2 contiguous limb leads or ≥2 mm in precordial. Localized by leads:
  - II, III, aVF: inferior (right coronary).
  - V1-V2: septal.
  - V3-V4: anterior.
  - V5-V6: lateral.
- **ST depression**: subendocardial ischemia or NSTEMI.
- **T-wave inversion**: ischemia, esp. with hyperacute T-waves preceding STEMI.
- **Q-waves**: pathological deep Q in established old infarct.
- **LBBB obscures** ischemic changes; new LBBB = STEMI equivalent.

**Long QT** (>460 ms): congenital or acquired (drugs, electrolyte abnormalities) → risk for torsades de pointes + sudden cardiac death.

question.question: Read an ECG: 1st-degree AV block detection
question.goal: An ECG shows: rate 65 bpm, P before every QRS, PR interval consistently 280 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, ST isoelectric. Diagnose.

steps.reveal: Yes — 65 bpm is in normal sinus rhythm range.
No — 280 ms is prolonged beyond normal upper limit of 200 ms. PR > 200 ms = AV-node conduction delay.

steps.prompt: Is every P-wave followed by a QRS?

steps.reveal: **1st-degree AV block** (PR > 200 ms with 1:1 conduction). Often benign — common in athletes, elderly. Causes: AV-node fibrosis, drugs (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin), Lyme disease, ischemia. No treatment needed unless symptomatic or progressing.

question.question: A patient presents with crushing chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
options: Right coronary artery (RCA). Inferior wall of left ventricle is supplied by RCA in ~85% of people (right-dominant circulation). ST elevation in II, III, aVF (inferior leads) indicates inferior MI. Treatment: rapid PCI within 90 minutes of presentation (door-to-balloon time). Add right-sided leads (V4R) to assess RV involvement; RV infarct (~30% of inferior MI) requires fluids + avoiding nitrates.
question.explanation:
**ECG-anatomy mapping for STEMI localization**:

| Leads | Wall | Artery |
|---|---|---|
| II, III, aVF | Inferior | RCA (85% right-dominant) or LCX (15% left-dominant) |
| V1, V2 | Septum | Proximal LAD (septal branches) |
| V3, V4 | Anterior | LAD (mid) |
| V5, V6 | Lateral | LCX or distal LAD |
| V7-V9 (posterior) | Posterior | Distal RCA or LCX |
| aVR (with diffuse ST depression) | Left main | LM disease (urgent) |

**RCA territory** (inferior wall):
- Inferior wall LV (lateral III, II, aVF)
- Right ventricle (V4R)
- Posterior wall (V7-V9; reciprocal ST depression in V1-V3)
- AV node (RCA supplies AV node in ~90% — RCA occlusion often causes 2°/3° AV block transiently)
- Sinus node (~60% RCA)

**Clinical management of STEMI**:
1. **Time critical**: 'time is muscle' — every 30 min delay = ~7% increase in 1-year mortality.
2. **Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor** (clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel) loaded.
3. **Anticoagulation** (heparin, bivalirudin).
4. **Primary PCI** within 90 min of first medical contact (door-to-balloon). Drug-eluting stent in culprit lesion.
5. **Thrombolytics** (TNK, alteplase) if PCI unavailable + within 12 hr of symptom onset.
6. **Post-MI**: beta-blocker, ACEi/ARB, statin, dual antiplatelet (DAPT) for 12+ months, MRA if HFrEF.
7. **Cardiac rehabilitation**.

**Mortality trends**: 30-day STEMI mortality fell from ~30% (1960s, no reperfusion) to ~5-7% (modern, with primary PCI). Massive impact of timely intervention + protocol-driven care.

hints: Which leads view the inferior wall?
slides.workedSolution: Inferior wall ST elevation (II, III, aVF) → RCA in 85% of patients (right-dominant circulation; LCX 15% in left-dominant). Treatment: primary PCI within 90 min. Assess RV involvement (V4R; ~30% of inferior MI); RV infarct requires fluids + nitrate avoidance. AV-node compromise common (RCA supplies AV node in ~90%); transient heart block requires monitoring.

question.question: Drag the slider to the upper limit of a normal PR interval (in ms).
question.explanation: Normal PR interval: 120-200 ms. > 200 ms = 1st-degree AV block. The PR interval measures conduction time from atrial depolarization (P-wave start) through AV node to ventricular depolarization (QRS start). AV node introduces ~100 ms delay; rest is conduction through atria + His-Purkinje system.

question.question: Order these arrhythmias by typical *clinical urgency* (least urgent to most urgent / lethal).
question.explanation:
Clinical urgency hierarchy:
• **1st-degree AV block**: often benign; observe, treat underlying cause if any.
• **Sinus tachycardia**: physiological (exercise, anxiety, fever) or pathological (sepsis, anemia, dehydration); rate-control underlying cause.
• **AFib (rate-controlled)**: stable; manage rate (beta-blocker, CCB) + anticoagulate to prevent stroke (CHADS-Vasc score → DOAC).
• **STEMI**: 'time is muscle'; primary PCI within 90 min. Every minute saved heart muscle. Life-threatening.
• **VFib**: lethal arrhythmia; immediate defibrillation (within minutes of arrest). Without defibrillation: 100% mortality. With prompt AED: 50-70% survival.

Learning to triage ECG findings + correlate with clinical context is core of emergency + critical care. Modern AI-augmented systems (Apple Watch, KardiaMobile) detect AFib + bradycardia in patients before symptoms; have prevented strokes + improved early detection.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how the long action-potential plateau in cardiac cells (vs neurons) prevents tetanic contraction of the heart.
question.rubric: Mentions: cardiac AP has ~200 ms plateau (Phase 2) maintained by Ca²⁺ inflow + K⁺ outflow balance. During plateau, voltage-gated Na channels are inactivated → cell is in absolute refractory period. Cannot be restimulated until plateau ends + channels recover (~300 ms total refractory). Compared to skeletal muscle: brief AP (~5 ms); summation + tetanic contractions possible with rapid stimulation. Why heart needs this: must contract once per cycle, fully relax + refill before next contraction. Tetanic heart contraction would prevent filling → no cardiac output → death. Long plateau is evolutionary solution. Some drugs target this: Class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol) prolong AP + QT; useful for some arrhythmias but risk torsades de pointes.
